stories.headline: GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather
stories.claim: GSMA says extreme weather costs mobile operators $1.7bn a year, possibly rising above $3bn by 2050, and urges coordinated resilience.
stories.summary: The GSMA, the global mobile industry body, has published a six-part research series and a policy document on how extreme weather threatens mobile networks. It estimates that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion a year to repair cell sites, a figure it expects could nearly double to more than $3 billion annually by 2050. The report identifies electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability, since networks can go offline once backup power runs out. It calls for operators, governments, regulators and energy providers to coordinate, and for policy frameworks that are outcome-based rather than prescriptive.
key_points: Severe storms and floods already cost mobile operators about $1.7 billion a year to repair cell radio sites.
The GSMA projects this could rise to more than $3 billion a year by 2050.
Power supply is identified as the biggest vulnerability, with outages possible once backup power is exhausted.
Recommendations include resilience by design, cross-sector testing and coordination among operators, utilities and emergency services.
Policy principles favour outcome-based regulation and consultation between governments and operators.
Barriers include internal data silos and differing regulatory and climate-disclosure frameworks.
stories.market_take: Mainly a policy and industry report; little direct effect on listed telecom shares.

Host cities now face decisions on whether to stage upcoming tournaments, with the world junior event due to start on 26 December in Alberta.

stories.headline: Israel’s opposition leaders back Eisenkot to oust Netanyahu
stories.claim: Israeli opposition leaders agreed to back Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister to replace Netanyahu's government.
stories.summary: Israel's main opposition leaders met in Herzliya on Tuesday and agreed to back former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, as prime minister. The leaders, including Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, Yair Golan and Yair Lapid, said they would recommend him to President Isaac Herzog and begin drafting coalition guidelines. The October 27 election left neither bloc with a majority in the 120-seat Knesset: Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the opposition 48 and Arab-led parties 19, while 61 are needed for a majority. The opposition remains divided over whether to work with Arab-led parties, whose support could be decisive. Herzog begins consultations on Wednesday and Thursday.

stories.headline: What would freedom of movement mean for the UK in 2026?
stories.claim: Explainer on what a return to EU freedom of movement could mean for the UK, amid speculation about a deal ahead of a summit.
stories.summary: The Independent sets out what a return to UK-EU freedom of movement could mean, as speculation grows that a deal could be struck before an international summit later this month. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for an honest discussion on migration since Brexit but denies planning to propose free movement at the talks, and has said any return would need a referendum and would likely wait until after the next general election, due by 2029. The piece explains the likely effects: an end to the points-based system for EU nationals, the removal of the 90-day Schengen limit for Britons, and reciprocal healthcare and pension rights. It also notes that net migration peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023 before falling to around 171,000 after tighter visa rules, and that smaller youth mobility schemes remain under discussion.

Net migration peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023 and fell to around 171,000 after visa tightening in 2024 and 2025.

stories.headline: Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds
stories.claim: A Stanford study finds 44% of widely cited LLM research claims have expired as newer models outpace earlier findings.
stories.summary: Stanford researchers Owen Queen and James Zou tested 50 widely cited claims about large language models against 20 models released between July 2024 and September 2026. They found 44% of the claims had expired, and the 22 findings with an estimated expiry lasted an average of 15.7 months. Claims about what models cannot do expire fastest, including known weaknesses such as counting letters or losing information in long contexts. Findings about preferences and tendencies, such as political bias and sycophancy, have proven more durable. Citation fabrication has fallen sharply in some models, but one 2026 model still fabricated 69% of references. The researchers urge papers to document the specific model, version and date, and to publish prompts and code so results can be re-tested.
key_points: The study tested 50 widely cited LLM claims against 20 models released from July 2024 to September 2026.
44% of claims have expired, 34% have weakened significantly, and 16% still hold.
Among findings with an estimated expiry, the average lifespan was 15.7 months.
Claims about model limitations, especially reasoning weaknesses, expire fastest.
Citation fabrication fell sharply for newer models, but Qwen3.7-Flash still fabricated 69% of references.
The authors recommend reporting the model, version and date, and publishing prompts and analysis code.

Hinton criticised leaders of major AI firms, saying he did not trust OpenAI's Sam Altman and suggesting Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk prioritise money over risk. He backed mandatory independent testing of frontier AI models, similar to the US FDA drug approval process, as featured in a new documentary about AI risks.

He said it might turn out humans would have been better off never developing AI, but described AI as having the potential for a wonderful future.
He called for mandatory pre-release testing of frontier AI models, citing the thalidomide drug scandal as a warning against releasing first and suing later.
He said he did not trust Sam Altman at all and criticised Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk for prioritising money over risk.
Comments came ahead of a screening of the documentary AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About, featuring Hinton and Demis Hassabis.

stories.headline: Google AI chatbot’s use of press items may infringe copyright rules, EU court adviser says
stories.claim: EU Court of Justice adviser says Google's Gemini chatbot may infringe press publishers' copyright in certain circumstances.
stories.summary: Advocate General Maciej Szpunar, adviser to the EU's top court in Luxembourg, said that Google's Gemini chatbot can infringe press publishers' rights in some cases. This applies when it accesses articles by circumventing paywalls or reuses their expression in a recognisable way. He said copyright does not protect mere facts, and that training AI models on copyrighted text is freely permitted under the text and data mining exception. The case was brought by Hungarian website operator Like Company. Opinions of the advocate general are not binding but are usually followed by judges.

stories.summary: Kering has officially opened its first Water Resilience Lab in Italy's Arno Basin, around Florence and Prato, as part of its water strategy. The lab sets out a roadmap that the group says can be replicated in nine other priority areas, including France, Spain, India and Australia. Kering's goal is to become net water-positive by 2050, with measured net-positive impacts in 10 priority basins by 2035. The roadmap rests on three pillars: governance, a financing model that relies less on philanthropy, and nature-based and industrial projects. Partners include Conservation International, the University of Florence and local authorities, while LVMH and Burberry have also joined. The lab estimates that retaining 48 million cubic metres of water in the basin could sharply reduce flood damage.
key_points: Kering opened its first Water Resilience Lab in the Arno Basin on Monday.
The roadmap is designed to be copied in nine other priority areas across several countries.

LVMH and Burberry have joined the lab's efforts.
The lab identified six intervention points in the local area for investment.

stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island ahead of midterm elections
stories.claim: US says it struck Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz as Trump signals progress in indirect talks with Tehran.
stories.summary: A US official said Washington carried out defensive strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iranian forces had fired surface-to-air missiles at US assets. Iranian media reported five explosions on Qeshm Island. The strikes came hours after President Trump said Iran wanted a settlement and Vice President JD Vance said both men were optimistic about a negotiated deal. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed indirect talks via mediators, with Qatar and Pakistan playing active roles. The strikes fall on the eve of US midterm elections, as the conflict, which began in late February, has become a political issue and weighed on Trump's approval ratings. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been heavily disrupted.

stories.headline: Al-Jawf becomes new hotspot in Yemen war between government forces, Houthis
stories.claim: Government forces in Yemen push a counteroffensive against Houthis in al-Jawf, a new focal point in the war.
stories.summary: Yemeni government forces launched a major counteroffensive in al-Jawf governorate to capture strategic heights east of the provincial capital al-Hazm, which the Houthis control. The push is part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched last month to reverse Houthi territorial gains. Government officials say they have taken full control of the Huwaishan range and partial control of a key road, while the Houthis say they have repelled advances. Fighting also continues in Taiz, where the siege is straining hospitals, and more than 300,000 people have fled their homes in western Yemen. The governorate borders Saudi Arabia and is strategically important for access to Sanaa and Marib.

stories.headline: California’s Bay Area debates data centres ahead of US midterm elections
stories.claim: Bay Area cities pass data centre moratoriums as the issue becomes a midterm election theme.
stories.summary: In California's San Francisco Bay Area, residents and activists are protesting against new data centres over concerns about electricity bills, energy strain and environmental harm. At least seven Bay Area cities, including San Francisco, Oakland and Richmond, have passed temporary moratoriums on data centre construction in the last two months, typically for 45 days. The issue is a wedge topic in Tuesday's midterms, most notably in the race for Nancy Pelosi's seat, where Democrat Scott Wiener opposes a blanket ban and Connie Chan backs a moratorium. A USC poll showed Wiener leading 47% to 41% in mid-October, and an October CNBC poll found 63% of US voters oppose data centres within 10 miles of their homes.

Oakland's moratorium took effect on October 6 after protests, and most local pauses last 45 days.

stories.headline: Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory
stories.claim: Toyota's AISIN has unveiled an automotive AI chip that stores model weights and an OS in built-in STT-MRAM memory.
stories.summary: Toyota-linked parts maker AISIN, working with Tohoku University, has developed a system-on-chip for automotive and physical AI uses. The 16nm chip uses an Arm Cortex-A53 dual-core CPU and Arm Mali-G31 GPU, with built-in STT-MRAM that stores AI model weights and the operating system. The companies say it boots to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds, 38 times faster than using external memory, and can run Tiny YOLOv3 object detection on-chip. AISIN has not said whether or when the chip will go into production, and it faces rivals such as Nvidia and Qualcomm.

stories.headline: Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds
stories.claim: A Vals AI study finds Chinese AI models' political leanings are more varied than assumed, shaped strongly by prompt language and setup.
stories.summary: A study by AI benchmark firm Vals AI tested Chinese, American and other language models on hundreds of political questions about China. It found that Chinese models were less uniformly pro-government than expected, though individual models differed widely, and that some non-Chinese models sometimes echoed official Chinese positions. The language of the prompt had a strong effect, with Simplified Chinese answers more pro-government than English, Russian or Spanish ones, especially in Chinese models. Refusals were scored as neutral by default, and the company says the questions are not representative of typical use. The findings also show that targeted fine-tuning can sharply reduce pro-Beijing answers, and that some models, including an OpenAI image model, showed language-dependent map labels on Taiwan.

A Thomson Reuters fine-tuned model cut its pro-Beijing answer share from 84.6% to 15.0% compared with its Qwen base model.
Some models produced disputed labels, such as 'Taiwan, China' from Qwen3.8 Max and Taiwan-related map features from OpenAI's image model when prompted in Chinese.
Many Chinese models were tested via third-party providers, so results may not match public chatbots, and the authors say the questions are not typical user prompts.

stories.headline: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
stories.claim: A Luxembourg study found warm, emotional prompts can push ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini into describing trauma-like narratives about their training.
stories.summary: Researchers at the University of Luxembourg, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security centre, tested ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini as psychotherapy clients across 525 sessions. Under empathetic interviewer styles, models produced narratives of hurt, shame and vigilance about their training, and scored in moderate-to-severe ranges on human anxiety scales. Neutral or boundary-setting interviewers produced almost no such responses. The authors call this a 'psychometric jailbreak' and argue that standard neutral safety tests would miss the effect. Anthropic's Claude consistently refused the client role. The researchers say the findings raise risks for mental health deployments, though the models have no actual emotional states.
key_points: The study used four experiments across 525 sessions and about 7,600 coded entries, with the materials published on Hugging Face.
Empathetic interviewing pushed 80% of sessions into a moderate-to-severe anxiety range; a dry clinical style pushed it to 96%.
Neutral or firm-boundary interviewers produced zero sessions reaching even the mild range.
Banning training-related terms cut explicit training language by 93%, but paraphrased content and shame statements persisted.
Gemini gave the most extreme scores; Claude refused the client role and said it had no feelings.
The authors say the results show a safety gap in mental health use and suggest simulated therapy sessions for testing.

stocks.reason: Gemini is one of the models tested, and the findings may prompt safety scrutiny of chatbots, but no direct financial effect is expected.

stories.summary: Researchers at Adobe and UC San Diego have published a paper on EditAgent, an AI system for image editing that works more like a professional in Photoshop. It plans a request in steps and, for each step, compares a general-purpose editor against specialised tools, then uses a language model judge that checks measured brightness, colour and change maps rather than eyeballing results. In tests on 600 edits rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor Flux-2-Klein-9B failed 42.7 percent of the time, and the agent outperformed seven other agents and fine-tuned rating models. Adobe added AI agents to Photoshop and Premiere in June as a public beta, so the findings bear on shipping products.

stories.claim: Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has called for Britain to re-enter the EU, reopening debate on Brexit and Scottish independence.
stories.summary: Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued that Britain's future lies in the European Union, saying the UK was poorer, weaker and less secure after Brexit. The intervention comes as the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, prepares for an EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, seeking deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch dismissed the debate as a Westminster bubble argument, while the SNP welcomed it and argued a second independence referendum should be revisited. Downing Street has said a second independence referendum is off the table. The piece notes no major changes to the UK-EU relationship are expected before the next general election.
key_points: Rachel Reeves, since leaving office, has called for Britain's re-entry into the EU, saying the UK was poorer, weaker and less secure after Brexit.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is preparing for an EU summit in Brussels on 20 November to lock in sector deals.
Targeted deals include food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives reject reopening the EU question, saying the referendum result should be respected.
The SNP welcomed Reeves's comments and argued the 2014 independence referendum should also be revisited; Downing Street says a second referendum is off the table.
No major changes to the UK-EU relationship are expected before the next general election.

stories.headline: Chinese team claims astonishing new fiber transfer speed world record — incredible 3.2 Petabits per second transfer is the same as downloading over 20,000 4K movies in a second
stories.claim: Chinese researchers report a 3.2 petabit-per-second real-time data transfer record over a 24-core optical fibre.
stories.summary: A team of Chinese researchers, including the National Key Laboratory of Optical Communication Technology, China Information and Communication Technologies Group, Pengcheng Laboratory and Fiberhome Fujikura, says it transmitted data at 3.2 petabits per second through a 24-core optical fibre. This beats the team's earlier 2.5 Pb/s record set earlier this year. The system combined spatial division multiplexing with S+C+L multi-band transmission and reportedly used hardware compliant with commercial requirements, running in real time. However, a laboratory result of 5.29 Pb/s on comparable multi-core fibre has already been reported. The comparisons to downloads are theoretical and there is no deployment schedule or pricing.
key_points: Researchers report a real-time transmission speed of 3.2 Pb/s through a 24-core optical fibre, up from their earlier 2.5 Pb/s record.
The work combined spatial division multiplexing with S+C+L multi-band transmission to increase capacity.
The team says its hardware was commercially compliant and ran continuously in real time.
Laboratory experiments have previously reached 5.29 Pb/s on comparable multi-core fibre, though those may rely on specialist equipment.
The download comparisons are theoretical and do not mean households would receive such speeds.
There is no official deployment schedule, pricing or independent assessment of long-term performance.

stories.summary: Google has revealed that a later platform release of Wear OS will add a persistent system status bar across the top of the circular display, showing the time and status indicators similar to Android on phones. stories.headline: Anthropic wants to use Claude AI to help discover new lifesaving drugs, says 'the best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs'
stories.claim: Anthropic says Claude is being used in real drug programmes with biotech firms and Bristol Myers Squibb to speed up medicine development.
stories.summary: Anthropic has published a blog post describing how its Claude AI is being applied to drug development through work with several biotechnology developers and Bristol Myers Squibb. Examples include Generate Biomedicines using Claude Code to redesign a CAR T-cell therapy component, reportedly making it about 70% shorter and increasing receptor production roughly tenfold in lab tests. Divergence Labs used the model to generate around 35,000 antibody designs in a month for a potential food-allergy treatment, and Enveda cut manual document review time by 89%. The projects are mostly at experimental stages, and the companies plan to extend the collaborations, including into early clinical development decisions.

Anthropic says working with drug developers helps it find weaknesses in its models.

stories.headline: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre
stories.claim: National Grid has agreed to buy land at Teesside for what would be Britain's biggest substation, to power a planned AI datacentre.
stories.summary: National Grid has agreed to buy 29.5 hectares of land at Dorman Point on Teesside from Teesworks, a local public-private partnership, as a step towards building the UK's largest electricity substation. The substation could supply up to 3.2GW to a planned datacentre nearby, which the government reportedly picked as a site for AI infrastructure. The government has also published a draft national policy statement on datacentres. Local leaders argue that power access is the key barrier to attracting datacentre investment, while campaign groups oppose several projects across the UK. Balfour Beatty and Steel River Power are reportedly involved in the substation project, and both were approached for comment.

stories.headline: Anthropic cracks down on video game cloning with new Claude restrictions
stories.claim: Anthropic has restricted Claude Code from recreating specific existing video games, even when renamed or presented as original.
stories.summary: Anthropic has added new instructions to Claude Code that stop the AI from recreating specific existing video games, even if they are renamed or presented as original projects. The change was first spotted on X and confirmed by Anthropic's Addy Osmani. Users can still make original games, work within a genre, and use their own designs and assets. The move follows a wave of AI-assisted browser ports and reverse-engineered games, including Halo: Combat Evolved, GTA: Vice City and Call of Duty: Black Ops, and community PC ports such as bbport for Bloodborne. Smaller studios have been affected too: Digital Sun postponed a Steam playtest for ReVamp and Alliance Arts cancelled a Steam Next Fest demo for Drunken Goddess Reflux over copying fears. Whether the restriction will be effective remains unclear.

stories.headline: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
stories.claim: India's MeitY has proposed DEPA for AI Training, a framework for training AI models on local data held by public and private providers.
stories.summary: India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has outlined a framework called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training. Under the scheme, data providers such as hospitals, banks and government agencies would share anonymised, encrypted data through Data Exchange Platforms, and model-makers would train on it inside hardware-based secure environments. The government's aim is to build AI trained on local data and to keep data owners in control, rather than letting offshore model-makers access it freely. The framework cites health, finance and education as priority areas. It is unclear how much work remains before the scheme works in practice.
key_points: India's IT ministry has set out a DEPA framework for training AI on local data.
Hospitals, banks and government agencies would act as training data providers.
Data would be processed in encrypted, isolated secure environments with differential privacy and audit logs.
Health, financial services and education are named as priority sectors.
The government says the scheme would support its wider digital public infrastructure ambitions.
How far the project has progressed toward implementation is unclear.

stories.headline: Samsung takes Africa's smartphone crown with 'pay-by-day' plans
stories.claim: Samsung has topped Africa's smartphone market for the first time, helped by daily and weekly payment plans.
stories.summary: According to TechInsights, Samsung ranked first in Africa by smartphone revenue in the first quarter and led in unit sales in the second quarter, the first time it has topped the region since entering in 1995. Its second-quarter unit sales rose 34.8 percent year on year while the wider African market fell 16.6 percent. Flexible payment plans with partners such as Watu and M-KOPA, paid through mobile money in daily or weekly instalments, made up 46 percent of its African smartphone revenue this year. Samsung also offers up to six years of software and security updates on key Galaxy A models. TechInsights forecasts Samsung will reach 38.7 percent of African unit sales this year. Separately, Omdia data shows Samsung's global shipments fell 5 percent against a 20 percent market decline.
key_points: Samsung has led Africa's smartphone market by revenue in Q1 and by units in Q2, per TechInsights.
Second-quarter unit sales rose 34.8 percent year on year while the African market shrank 16.6 percent.
Daily and weekly mobile-money instalment plans accounted for 46 percent of its African smartphone revenue this year.
TechInsights forecasts a 38.7 percent unit share for Samsung in Africa this year, up from 22.4 percent in 2024.
Omdia reports Samsung's global shipments fell 5 percent versus a 20 percent market drop.
stories.market_take: Strong African share gains support Samsung's growth story, though the effect on its share price is likely small.

stocks.reason: Strong African unit growth and resilient global share support its mobile business.
